results.title: Understanding Minimum Detectable Effect in AB Testing
results.content: The Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) is the smallest true effect an A/B test can detect with sufficient statistical power, factoring in test duration, sample size and practical significance. ***The answer is that the MDE is about the true effect, whereas the result you get from the test is the observed effect.***. That said, if your calculations tell you that you’re going to need an MDE of 20% and up, then that’s likely a sign that it’s too soon to start A/B testing. There’s practical significance, how much it would cost to implement a winning variant, how long you’d need to run the test to achieve that MDE, how likely you are to get wins that exceed your MDE by a healthy margin, and how comfortable you are with the risk of missing true effects (false negatives) and of implementing changes that aren’t actually better than the original (false positives).

results.title: What is Minimum Detectable Effect in A/B Testing?
results.content: **The Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE)** is a crucial concept in experiment design and A/B testing. Understanding the MDE is essential for effective hypothesis testing and ensuring your experiments have sufficient statistical power. The smaller the MDE, the more subtle changes your experiment can detect. ## The Relationship Between MDE and Statistical Power. Here's how MDE and statistical power work together:. 1. If you want to detect a smaller MDE, you'll need a larger sample size to maintain the same level of statistical power. 2. If you have a fixed sample size, you may need to accept a larger MDE to maintain sufficient statistical power. There are various online calculators and tools available to help you determine the MDE for your experiments. The Minimum Detectable Effect is a fundamental concept in experimentation and A/B testing. By understanding and correctly applying MDE in your experiment design and data analysis, you can ensure that your tests are properly powered and capable of detecting meaningful changes.

results.title: Understanding Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) – VWO
results.content: Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) is a critical concept in any type of testing. By setting a smaller MDE, you can reduce the undetectable range and make your test more sensitive to smaller changes in the conversion rate. * **Balance Sensitivity and Practicality**: While it's tempting to set a very low MDE to detect even minor improvements, this can lead to impractically large sample sizes and extended test durations. Conversely, a larger MDE is preferred for sensitive metrics to detect even minor positive effects. + **Sensitive Metrics (e.g., Time Spent on Page):** These metrics are more prone to change, making it easier to detect positive effects with a larger MDE. + **Optimize test duration:** Adjusting the MDE as the test progresses can help balance the need for detecting smaller effects with the practical constraints of time and resources. MDE helps you strike the right balance between detecting meaningful changes and ensuring your tests are efficient and cost-effective.

results.title: Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects
results.content: # Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects. Power is sometimes also called “sensitivity.” Power refers to the ability of a test (i.e., an analysis of an experiment) to detect a “true effect” that is different from the null hypothesis (e.g., the ability to detect a difference between treatment and control when that difference actually exists). There are four factors that influence power: sample size, the true effect size, the variance of the effect, and the alpha-threshold (level of significance). If we have a more liberal threshold (i.e., a higher alpha level), we have more power to detect the effect. MDE tell us what is the smallest true effect, in standard deviations of the outcome, that is detectable for a given level of power and statistical significance. Because the standard deviation is influenced by sample size, MDE incorporates all of the information of a power calculation but does so in a way that applies to all experiments.
